title: Do Political Parties Matter? Evidence from U.S. Cities
research_question: Do the partisan affiliations of elected chief executives in U.S. cities causally affect local policy outcomes, including the size of local government, the composition of public spending across functions such as police, fire, and parks, and local crime rates? Additionally, does holding local executive office confer a political advantage to the incumbent's party in subsequent elections, and what features of the urban environment moderate any partisan influence on policy?
data_description: The authors assembled a new panel data set from a survey sent to all U.S. cities and townships with populations of at least 25,000 as of 2000, collecting information on the timing, candidates, vote totals, party affiliations, and electoral characteristics of mayoral races from 1950 to 2005. The final analytic sample comprises 4,543 mayoral elections in 413 cities, with regression analyses restricted to 1,993 elections from 1968-2004 between Democrats and Republicans. These election records are merged with local public finance data from the Historical Data Base of Individual Government Finances (Census of Governments and Annual Survey of Governments), covering revenues, taxes, expenditures, employment, and spending shares on wages, police, fire, and parks. City-level violent and property crime rates (murders, robberies, burglaries, larcenies per 1,000 residents) come from FBI Uniform Crime Reporting data. Demographic and economic city characteristics are drawn from the 2000 Census.
institutional_context: U.S. mayoral elections provide a setting to examine whether partisan control of local executive office shapes policy. Cities differ from state and federal jurisdictions in important ways: they are far smaller and more demographically and politically homogeneous than congressional districts, and residents face low costs of relocating to competing nearby municipalities within the same metropolitan area. These features of fragmented metropolitan areas—spatial sorting into homogeneous communities and inter-jurisdictional competition—may constrain politicians' ability or incentive to deviate from moderate, centrist policies, even if mayors hold strong partisan preferences. Additionally, roughly 59% of cities with populations above 25,000 hold institutionally non-partisan elections, prohibiting party labels on ballots, though many such races still feature partisan candidates. Mayors also lack the disciplinary mechanisms (such as committee assignments or party campaign funds) that party leaders use to enforce partisan discipline at higher levels of government. The authors collected party affiliation data from city/county clerks, voter registration records, and local newspaper archives to overcome non-partisan ballot conventions.
